newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-U.S. tax bill focus shifts to Senate.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-U.S. tax bill focus shifts to Senate.

text.p: The focus on tax legislation shifts to the Senate next week where a key Republican plans to unveil his version of how to cut taxes by a net $85 billion over 5 years.
The House Ways and Means Committee Friday approved a tax cut bill that will ultimately have to be reconciled with the Senate version.

Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, was scheduled to unveil his plan Tuesday of how to implement the tax portion of the balanced budget agreement reached between congressional leaders and the White House.
White House unhappiness with the bill passed by the House committee will also have to be dealt with at some point.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich said Republicans will have to negotiate with President Clinton to get a tax bill he will sign, but that did not mean they would accept a major rewrite.
"We will sit down with the president's folks and with the president and try to reach an accomodation on issues of great importance to the president," Gingrich said.
But the Georgia Republican said that as long as the bill conformed to the overall budget agreement made with Clinton, "I don't think we have an obligation" to let the White House rewrite it.
The White House has already begun mounting a campaign for changes in the congressional tax legislation.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton found several aspects of the legislation "quite objectionable."

"The Ways and Means bill included, despite the protests of the president ... some of those very features he considers quite objectionable. This is not the bill that's going to be signed into law," McCurry said.
An outline of proposals that Roth is considering putting into his legislation showed similarity with the House bill on education tax initiatives that the White House is raising objections about.
The outline showed the Senate Finance Committee proposal for Clinton's HOPE scholarship tax credit would, like the House bill, be a 50 percent tax credit for up to $3,000 of college tuition expenses.

Clinton's proposal would have made it a straight $1,500 tuition tax credit for higher education. Administration officials have said the congressional legislation would penalize students attending less-expensive schools like community colleges who might not get the full $1,500.
The education tax initiatives in the broad Senate Finance Committee outline were given a preliminary cost estimate of $30 billion over five years.
The White House has already raised a ruckus over the fact that in the House legislation, education tax initiatives were below the $35 billion over five years that Clinton sought.
The balanced budget agreement had said "roughly" $35 billion should be included for education tax initiatives.
The Senate Finance Committee outline also included a capital gains tax cut to 20 percent from the current maximum of 28 percent for individuals, the same as in House legislation.
It did not have anything for a corporate capital gains tax cut. The House bill would gradually cut the corporate capital gains tax rate to 30 percent from the current 35 percent.
The Senate Finance outline included expanding Individual Retirement Accounts (IRA), which has been a priority for Roth.
It had a proposed $500 per child tax credit that would cost an estimated $83 billion over five years. That would be a higher cost than the $71 billion in the House Ways and Means Committee bill.
The child credit would be allowed for children under age 17 and parents with children aged 13-16 would be required to deposit the credit into an education IRA.
A proposal in both bills for estate tax relief would phase in a higher threshold where the inheritance tax kicks in, to $1 million from the current $600,000.
Gingrich said he expected the measure from the House Ways and Means Committee would pass the House.
